zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical review aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0; supplied page subset). Used for lexical cross-checks after reading the BnF scan, not as authority for this copy's spelling, typography, or placement. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: The opening fragment continues Fo- on f0244 to form the Buddha example, ending in coroſu, 'kill.' The following Portuguese starts the separate offence of killing one's father and mother; the preceding catchword is not an additional body word.
Bumouo coroſu supplies the example for killing parents. The new Portuguese clause then begins the offence of killing a penitential or holy person, with ho- continuing on the next row.
The Portuguese completes 'penitential or holy man'; Aracanuo is the object of the following killing verb and refers to an arhat. Keep the printed ſancto and the example on their physical lines.

runs.text: De tirar ſangue do Fotoque. Vt,

lines.note: The scan has coroſu, including a faint second o omitted by OCR. The next offence is drawing blood from the Buddha; Fotoque is embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation.

Fotoqeno miyori chiuo nagaſu means to shed blood from the Buddha's body. Preserve the visibly tight Dema- at the start of the next Portuguese clause rather than inserting a lexical boundary into the print.
The final clause concerns killing a religious person; Xucqeuo gaiſuru gives the Japanese example. The initial tar completes matar across the physical break.
Goguiacuzai denotes the same five grave offences. The example starts here with the object marker uo separated in the print and continues with the verb below.
Tçucuru completes the example 'commit these five aforesaid sins.' Preserve the historical spelling peccados and the lower-case continuation of the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Cinco partes, ou materiaes de que ſe

lines.note: This Goguiǒ entry concerns the five constituent materials, not the homonymous herb below. The Portuguese definition introduces the list of substances composing mixed bodies.

The list begins with wood, fire and earth. The introductory i, is upright with the Japanese enumeration, not part of the italic Portuguese; the nasal spelling compoẽ is retained. No comma is attached after do on this physical row.

Gon and ſui complete the enumeration with metal and water. A separate comma is clearly printed beside the right column rule on this same row; it is recorded at the far right rather than silently moved to the preceding do.
The second Goguiǒ is defined only as an herb. The scan supports the caron and nasal abbreviation Hũa; no botanical identification is added to the diplomatic text.

runs.text: Hum dos graos, ou dignidades que dà

lines.note: Go-i names a rank or dignity conferred by the Dairi. Its internal hyphen distinguishes the adjacent vowels and is not a line-end division.
This row completes the preceding definition with the Dairi as the grantor of the rank. Dairi is a Japanese title inside the Portuguese explanation and remains in the observed italic run.
The gloss reads 'sins, faults,' not OCR ouloas. Gôin and Xiuaza chinamu introduce the causal consequences of deeds, explained in the following lines through the compilers' account of rebirth.

runs.text: ou penas que hum recebe neſta vida pellos ma-

lines.note: The definition describes penalties received in this life for earlier wrongs. The final ma- starts males on the next line; the printed pellos is retained.

runs.text: les que fez noutro nacimento como cuidaõ os gen

lines.note: The earlier wrongs are assigned to another birth, as the people described by the compilers supposedly believe. Keep nacimento and cuidaõ, and do not invent a hyphen after the unhyphenated gen at the right edge.

Tios completes gentios across the line break. Gôin no vomoi fitogia begins an example about a person burdened with heavy consequences of past deeds. The second pass confirms a visible word gap between Gôin and no, unlike the joined OCR reading.

runs.text: homem que eſtà enredado em muitos peccados,

lines.note: The Portuguese calls this a person entangled in many sins. This is part of the example's gloss, not a fresh definition; the scan retains the grave accent in eſtà.

runs.text: ou penas pollas culpas paßadas feitas noutra

lines.note: Alternatively the example describes penalties for past faults committed in another age. Preserve pollas and the ß in paßadas rather than modernizing their spelling.
Idade completes the reference to an earlier age or life. This short continuation belongs to the Gôin example above, not to the next headword.
The scan reads Goin and coye, not Coin and coxe, and shows a comma after tons. Itçutçuno coye means five voices; the Portuguese initially explains musical voices or tones.

runs.text: ou toadas conforme ao vſo da muſica de Iapão.

lines.note: The tones are described according to Japanese musical usage. Retain the historical Portuguese vſo, muſica and Iapão without adding an identification of a particular scale.

runs.text: ¶ Item, As cinco vogais de Iapão.

lines.note: A separate sense identifies the five Japanese vowels. The opening A. is printed after a conspicuously wide gap at the far right of this row and is preserved there; the remaining four labels continue on the next physical line.

The scan has the remaining four capital vowel labels I, V, YE and VO, all in the italic run; OCR lowered I and omitted the final O. Together with A above, these are the dictionary's own vowel notation, not modern kana or IPA.
Goiſagui is described as a kind of grey heron. Retain the long ſ in the headword and the source's broad bird description rather than adding a species name.
The damaged initial word reads Gôja, not Ciôja. Famano maſago is sand on the shore, matching the Portuguese; the circumflex and the spelling Areas remain as printed.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Permet. Muitos como areas da

lines.note: The added metaphorical sense means numerous like the sands of the shore. Preserve the compact label Permet. and the physical division before praya.
Praya completes the shore-sand comparison. This is the end of the Gôja entry rather than a separate headword or a catchword.
Goje is glossed simply as a blind woman. No musical occupation is supplied because it is not stated in this entry; the old spelling Molher is retained.
Gojen with Von maye denotes being before a noble person. The final n is clear here and provides a useful local comparison with the damaged last letter in the following headword.

runs.text: Meſa com comer pera peßoa honrada.

lines.note: The gloss concerns a table or meal for an honoured person, identifying the gozen meal sense. The printed final letter is worn to a u-like form, unlike the clear n above; Gojeu is retained as the visible, provisionally chosen reading rather than silently normalized to Gojen.
Gojimeqi and its abbreviated forms describe making a noise while chewing. Preserve the printed eita form and the short s in mastigando; the foods being chewed are specified below.
The foods are raw and hard, completing the definition of noisy chewing. The row is an indented continuation, with no extra Japanese entry supplied.

runs.text: Gojǒ. i, Iin, gui, rei, chi, xin.

lines.note: Gojǒ introduces the five moral virtues, enumerated as Iin, gui, rei, chi and xin. The enumeration is Japanese explanatory material, not words embedded in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: bons cuſtumes, ou virtudes moraes, & politi-

lines.note: The Portuguese calls them good customs or moral and political virtues. The final politi- belongs with cas on the next row, and the spelling cuſtumes remains unchanged.

runs.text: cas, de que tratão os Chinas, & Iapões.

lines.note: The definition attributes discussion of these virtues to the Chinese and Japanese. Preserve the source's names Chinas and Iapões and the nasal spelling tratão.
Gǒjǒ, marked as Buddhist terminology, is explained by Auaxe naſu: joining or composing. Both carons are visible; this is a distinct entry from the five virtues immediately above.
The Portuguese completes 'joining or composition'; Xidai gǒjǒno ye- begins the example about a body compounded of the four elements. Preserve the example's line-final hyphen.
Xin completes the preceding Japanese fragment; the Portuguese describes this body as borrowed and composed of elements. Preserve the scan's empreſtado and unhyphenated composto.
The four elements complete the bodily-composition example. They should not be harmonized with the separate five-material Goguiǒ entry earlier in the column.
Gojǒracu, explained by Gacuno na, is the name of a particular song or piece of music. The nasal abbreviation and the final cã- are preserved across the break.
To completes canto, followed by the alternative 'music.' This short row finishes the musical-title entry without introducing further terminology.

Mauo cudaſu means subduing the demon, and the Buddhist gloss begins with humiliation. At enlargement a faint V-shaped mark survives above o, supporting Gǒma; this low-contrast caron is a chosen but nonblocking uncertainty. No hyphen is visible after Humilha.

runs.text: ção, & rogo que o Diabo fez a Xaca quando o

lines.note: The Portuguese continues with the humiliation and supplication made to Shaka by the figure it calls the Devil. Xaca is visibly upright within the italic explanation; this records the compilers' religious account rather than endorsing its terminology.

runs.text: vencia algũas vezes como ſe conta em ſeus

lines.note: The account continues with occasions of defeat, as related in the books being referenced. Preserve the nasal abbreviation algũas and the syntax across the physical lines.
Liuros closes the source-attribution clause in the Gǒma explanation. It is body text, not bottom furniture, and remains separately cropped from the lower rule.

runs.text: Iergelim de que ſe faz azeite.

lines.note: This Goma means sesame, from which oil is made. The scan separates faz and azeite; retain the historical Iergelim rather than modernizing the plant name.

runs.text: Certa ceremonia que os Xingonjùs fa-

lines.note: The next Goma is a rite performed by the Shingon group named Xingonjùs. Correct OCR ceremnonia to the clearly printed ceremonia; the printed grave-like accent in the group name is retained, not replaced from modern pronunciation.
The compilers describe the ceremony in their own terms as a supplication to the Devil. Gomauo begins the Japanese example, while deprecandoo remains joined as printed.

runs.text: Fazer eſta ceremonia botando no fogo a

lines.note: Taqu completes 'perform or burn the goma rite.' The Portuguese describes placing substances in a fire; retain the unhyphenated a that begins azeite across this physical break.

runs.text: zeite de Goma, & caſca de loureiro, &c.

lines.note: The substances are sesame oil and laurel bark, followed by '&c.' Goma is the Japanese word embedded in this Portuguese explanation and is printed in its italic run.
Gomei is equated with Vǒgui and glossed as a fan. The V plus caron-marked o is visible; the Japanese synonym after i, is not a Portuguese-embedded typeface term.

runs.text: Hũa certa pelle branda de cor roxa,

lines.note: Gomen is a certain soft purple skin or leather. The damaged o remains compatible with the repeated Gomenno below; preserve Hũa and the colour word roxa.

runs.text: de que ſe fazem Tabis de molheres, ou luuas.

lines.note: The leather is used to make women's tabi or gloves. Tabis is embedded in the Portuguese and appears italic, including the lower-case letters; its plural s is retained.
Gomenno caua is an alternative expression for the same leather. The paragraph sign introduces that expression, and Idem refers back to the preceding description.

runs.text: Gomi. Itçutçuno agiuai. i, ſuxi, nigaxi,

lines.note: Gomi means five tastes, introduced by Itçutçuno agiuai. The enumeration starts with sour and bitter, ſuxi and nigaxi; preserve the long ſ and the historical agiuai.
Amaxi, caraxi and xiuafayuxi complete the five tastes with sweet, pungent and saline. The narrow, worn f in xiuafayuxi is retained rather than changed to t from its residual cross stroke.

runs.text: ou ſabores. ſ. Azedo, amargo, doce, que

lines.note: The Portuguese begins its own list: sour, bitter, sweet and the taste 'that' burns. Preserve the printed abbreviation ſ. and carry que into requeima below.
The list completes pungency with requeima, then adds brackish or naturally salty. This finishes the five-taste definition; no extra sixth taste is introduced by the alternative Portuguese wording.

runs.text: Lodo que eſtà misturado na agoa turua.

lines.note: This separate Gomi is mud suspended in turbid water. The scan supports the short s in misturado and the grave accent in eſtà; keep agoa and turua as printed.
Gomiga tatçu describes mud rising or being stirred up. The indented paragraph example belongs to the muddy-water sense, with Aleuantarſe retaining its historical initial spelling.
The first gloss includes river silt; Gomiga ita then illustrates the mud having settled. Preserve ita as printed and the line-final a- that continues aſentado.

runs.text: ſentado o lodo. ¶ Item, Vaza de rio, ou

lines.note: The settling gloss ends, and a further sense gives river or sea sediment. Keep the source's single long ſ in the continued aſentado and the paragraph boundary before Item.

runs.text: mar. ¶ Itẽ, Permet. Polme de Cha gros-

lines.note: The entry extends metaphorically to thick tea pulp. Cha is a Japanese term inside the Portuguese explanation; the scan shows a word boundary before gros-, whose second s continues below. Preserve Itẽ and Permet.
The thick tea is dissolved in hot water; Chano go- begins a Japanese example about its appearance. Keep the Portuguese long ſ at the continuation and the hyphen dividing gomi.

runs.text: A cor do polme do Cha he boa.

lines.note: The example says that the colour of the tea pulp is good. Cha is embedded in the Portuguese gloss, whereas mi iroga yoi is the continuation of the standalone Japanese example.

runs.text: Cãja cõ Xiru feito de cinco miſturas.

lines.note: Gomijucu is a gruel or soup preparation with five ingredients, described using Xiru. Preserve the nasal abbreviations Cãja and cõ; Xiru is a Japanese word embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation.
Gomocuyu is a wash or decoction made with five medicinal woods. The scan retains Lauatorio and the nasal cõ, with cin- continuing onto the next row.
Co completes cinco, followed by the medicinal woods. This is a continuation of the preparation's definition, not a further headword.
Gǒmon concerns coercive interrogation or torture, explained by Araqenaqu xeme tô. Preserve the caron of Gǒmon and the distinct circumflex in tô; the source's Tratos is the historical gloss.
Gǒmon caxacu ſuru illustrates administering torments or torture. The caron remains visible, and the definition continues on the next physical line.
The stated purpose is to make someone confess. The scan uses the ß form in confeßar; this is a historical dictionary gloss, not an instruction being supplied by the review.
Gǒmô with Qeno ſaqi denotes the tips of hairs. Preserve the contrasting caron and circumflex; the terminal S. is an upright usage label, not part of the italic definition.
Gǒna is described only as a kind of shellfish. The caron is visible above the worn o; no narrower zoological identity is imposed on the brief gloss.

runs.text: Dentro da comarca, ou territorio que ha

lines.note: Gǒnai means within a district or territory. The caron is clear; the administrative explanation continues below rather than ending at ha.

runs.text: na diuiſão dos reinos de Iapão.

lines.note: The territory is situated within the divisions of Japan's realms. Keep diuiſão, reinos and Iapão in the diplomatic transcription rather than substituting modern administrative names.
Gonbin concerns the voice or manner of speech, explained with Cotobano couairouo yǔ. The caron in yǔ is visible, and Vt introduces the example on the next row.
The example describes speaking clearly and pleasantly. Retain the printed zauayacani rather than normalizing it to a modern form; the worn last n of Gonbin is read with the headword directly above.

runs.text: com eloquencia, & bom metal de voz.

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies eloquence and a good quality or timbre of voice. Metal de voz is the source's expression; preserve the spelling and sentence punctuation.
Gonca, explained by Cotobano xita, concerns the moment immediately after speaking. Its definition begins 'on finishing' and continues with dizer below.
The alternatives emphasize immediacy and speed. Gonca starts the illustrative phrase; retain the ß in depreßa and the physical separation of the example across rows.
Ni qiuo ſatoru completes the example of immediately grasping an intention. The Portuguese begins 'guess what someone wants,' with hum preserved as printed.

runs.text: dizer, ou tem no coração logo em dizendo a

lines.note: The gloss concerns what the speaker means or has in mind as soon as a word is uttered. Preserve the carried syntax and the aligned reading à; the tiny accent at the right edge is weak.
Palaura completes the preceding example's explanation. This short body continuation is not an independent entry or a displaced catchword.
Gonchǔ, explained by Cotobano vchi, means within words or in the course of speech. The marked final vowel and the line-ending pala- are visible.
Uras completes palauras, followed by 'while speaking.' Preserve the unmodernized spelling and the indentation that associates this row with Gonchǔ.
Goncu is a word or sentence. The example begins Gon- and continues as cuuo below; keep the printed hyphen instead of joining the physical lines.
Goncuuo tçugu is paraphrased by Cotobauo tçuzzuquru, joining or continuing words. The final Fa starts Portuguese Falar without a printed hyphen, which is therefore not supplied.

runs.text: lar, ou enfiar as palauras, ou ſentenças.

lines.note: The explanation gives speaking or stringing words and sentences together. The beginning lar completes Fa above, and the original spelling palauras remains unchanged.
Goncuni tçumaru and goncuga nai describe becoming stuck for words or having nothing to say. The roman l, separates alternatives; it is not the digit one.

runs.text: Ficar conuencido ſem falar palaura como nal-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes being refuted and left speechless, for example in a dispute. Preserve conuencido in that contextual sense and the line-final nal-.
Gũa completes nalgũa, followed by diſputa and '&c.' This closes the speechless-in-dispute example without adding an extra paragraph or heading.
Gônẽ with Tçuneno coto means an ordinary or habitual thing. Keep its circumflex and nasal tilde; the terminal S. is upright, and the signature and catchword below are separate page furniture.
The far-right catchword reads Gongo followed by a comma. The separately positioned H b to its left is a signature, not part of the catchword.
